newsitem.title: USA: Judge backs tests on King assassination gun.
newsitem.headline: Judge backs tests on King assassination gun.

text.p: A judge on Thursday backed new tests on the rifle purportedly used to kill Martin Luther King Jr. in 1968, a move that could lead to a trial for the civil rights leader's convicted assassin.

The ruling pumped fresh energy into the conspiracy speculation that has dogged the tragedy for three decades. But it was problematic whether James Earl Ray -- who confessed to killing King and then denied it -- would ever get his day in court.
The 68-year-old Ray is seriously ill with liver disease that may kill him in a matter of weeks.
Thursday's ruling, which itself could be challenged, was only a recommendation that a state appeals court drop its 1994 order blocking any ballistics tests.

The ruling by Judge Joseph Brown in Shelby County Criminal Court hinged on a new state law which states that closed cases may be re-opened if there is a reasonable possibility that new scientific tests not available at the time of the crime can prove a person's innocence, the judge told reporters in explaining his decision. DNA evidence has been used to exonerate convicted murderers, he noted.

Ray's lawyers contended that sophisticated tests involving the use of an electron microscope could magnify details on the fatal bullet and the rifle on which Ray's fingerprints were found and show it was not the murder weapon.

But John Campbell, assistant district attorney for the county, told reporters that anyone who thinks Ray will ever come to trial is "hallucinating ... we know several of the witnesses are dead and 30 years later it would be difficult to present the evidence."

Because Ray pleaded guilty 11 months after the slaying he avoided a trial and possible death sentence. He was sentenced to 99 years in jail, but changed his story almost immediately and said he was a dupe for a mysterious accomplice who actually did the shooting.
King's widow Coretta and son Dexter both offered emotional testimony in favour of reopening the case on Thursday.
William Pepper, Ray's lead attorney, told the court that Ray "has always alleged that the rifle in evidence is not the murder weapon, but a throw-down gun."
A firearms testing expert brought by Pepper testified that the soft-point lead bullet, now fragmented, that killed King was still "in good condition" for testing and "not deformed."

The original ballistics examinations done by the FBI and tests done a decade later for the House investigative committee came up with inconclusive results when they tried to match the fatal bullet with the rifle. Even test-fired bullets could not be matched to the rifle, a result that experts testified was rare but not unknown, especially with a high-powered rifle like the one purportedly used to kill King.

King's widow Coretta and son Dexter looked on as Pepper said: "In the 28-year history of this case, (Ray) has never had the right to test this rifle. The defence has never had the right to have access to FBI test fire worksheet reports nor House Select Committee test fire worksheet reports.
"What we are seeking here for the first time ... is an opportunity to test this rifle in an effort to exclude it for all time as the murder weapon."

A congressional panel concluded that Ray was the sole assassin, possibly motivated by a bounty placed on King's head by a small group of racists. Pepper has said that he believed King was shot by someone hiding in a bush outside the rooming house and that the slaying was a plot that involved the Mafia. Other conspiracy theorists have blamed the FBI and even the U.S. military.
